plan.contextChunk: This figure compares two competing models of enzyme–substrate binding through four sequential diagrams arranged in two panels: panel (a) for the lock-and-key model and panel (b) for the induced fit model. In panel (a), the left diagram shows a green enzyme with a rigid, pre-formed active site cavity labeled 'Active site is proper shape,' with two complementary-shaped purple substrate molecules (labeled 'Substrates') positioned above it ready to fit precisely into the cleft; the right diagram shows the resulting 'Substrate complex formed' with the substrates seated snugly in the geometrically unchanged active site. In panel (b), the left diagram shows the enzyme with a more open and flexible active site labeled 'Active site changes to fit,' indicating a conformational adjustment upon substrate approach; the right diagram shows the 'Substrate complex formed' after the enzyme has reshaped itself to wrap tightly around the substrate. Both models account for substrate specificity — only a structurally compatible molecule can bind the active site — but differ in whether that specificity arises from a rigid pre-formed pocket or from an adaptive conformational change induced by substrate binding. This figure introduces enzyme active-site specificity at the molecular level and sets up the comparison of lock-and-key versus induced-fit mechanisms as competing explanations for how enzymes selectively bind and catalyze reactions with particular substrates.

interactionPlan.concept: Enzyme specificity arises from the complementary fit between substrate and active site — either as a rigid pre-formed pocket (lock-and-key) or as a flexible pocket that reshapes itself upon binding (induced fit).

demo_steps.title: Free enzyme and substrates
demo_steps.narration: A green enzyme sits below two purple substrate molecules. Hover any part to name it: enzyme body, active site cleft, and the small colored contact patches that must match.

demo_steps.title: Lock-and-key: the pocket is already right
demo_steps.narration: Drag binding progress forward. The substrates descend and slot in, but trace the cleft outline — it never moves. The active site is a rigid, pre-formed shape.

demo_steps.title: Switch to induced fit, unbound
demo_steps.narration: Now the same enzyme is drawn with a shallower, more open cleft — it does not yet match the substrates. Under lock-and-key logic, nothing should bind here.

demo_steps.title: Induced fit: the pocket closes in
demo_steps.narration: Sweep the slider again. As the substrates approach, the enzyme's surface deforms and wraps around them — the dashed ghost shows where the cleft used to be.

demo_steps.title: Compare the two complexes
demo_steps.narration: Play the docking animation in each mode back to back. Both end in a tight substrate complex — the difference is whether the enzyme had to move to get there.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Specificity does not require a rigid pocket — in induced fit the enzyme earns its complementary shape only after the correct substrate arrives, so the fit is a consequence of binding rather than a precondition for it.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single enzyme–substrate scene centered on a light background, with a model-name caption beneath ('(a) Lock-and-key model' / '(b) Induced fit model'). Enzyme: large pale yellow-green rounded trapezoid with a thick dark olive outline, flat bottom, domed shoulders, and a notched cleft in the top surface; label 'Enzyme' below it. Two purple (lavender fill, dark purple outline) substrate shapes float above: the left one boxy with a rectangular peg, the right one rounder with a tapered peg, each peg tipped in a dusty pink/tan patch that mirrors a matching patch inside the cleft. Black wedge arrows point from the substrates down into the notch; a 'Substrates' label with two thin leader lines sits above. A center text label reads 'Active site is proper shape' in lock-and-key mode and 'Active site changes to fit' in induced-fit mode; at full binding it becomes 'Substrate complex formed', and the two substrates meet along a thick black vertical seam. In lock-and-key the cleft geometry is identical at progress 0 and 1; in induced fit the cleft starts shallow and open and the olive outline visibly curls inward to hug the substrates as progress increases, with a dashed gray ghost of the original contour optionally overlaid. Keep line weights heavy and cartoon-like, matching the textbook's flat-color style.

authoredContext:
Enzyme molecules possess an active site, a part of the molecule with a shape that allows it to bond to a specific substrate (a reactant molecule), forming an enzyme-substrate complex as a reaction intermediate. There are two models that attempt to explain how this active site works. The most simplistic model is referred to as the lock-and-key hypothesis, which suggests that the molecular shapes of the active site and substrate are complementary, fitting together like a key in a lock. The induced fit hypothesis, on the other hand, suggests that the enzyme molecule is flexible and changes shape to accommodate a bond with the substrate. This is not to suggest that an enzyme’s active site is completely malleable, however. Both the lock-and-key model and the induced fit model account for the fact that enzymes can only bind with specific substrates, since in general a particular enzyme only catalyzes a particular reaction ( ).

(a) According to the lock-and-key model, the shape of an enzyme’s active site is a perfect fit for the substrate. (b) According to the induced fit model, the active site is somewhat flexible, and can change shape in order to bond with the substrate.

A diagram is shown of two possible interactions of an enzyme and a substrate. In a, which is labeled “Lock-and-key,” two diagrams are shown. The first shows a green wedge-like shape with two small depressions in the upper surface of similar size, but the depression on the left has a curved shape, and the depression on the right has a pointed shape. This green shape is labeled “Enzyme.” Just above this shape are two smaller, irregular, lavender shapes each with a projection from its lower surface. The lavender shape on the left has a curved projection which matches the shape of the depression on the left in the green shape below. This projection is shaded orange and has a curved arrow extending from in to the matching depression in the green shape below. Similarly, the lavender shape on the right has a projection with a pointed tip which matches the shape of the depression on the right in the green shape below. This projection is shaded orange and has a curved arrow extending from in to the matching depression in the green shape below. Two line segments extend from the depressions in the green shape to form an inverted V shape above the depressions. Above this and between the lavender shapes is the label, “Active site is proper shape.” The label “Substrates” is at the very top of the diagram with line segments extending to the two lavender shapes. To the right of this diagram is a second diagram showing the lavender shapes positioned next to each other, fit snugly into the depressions in the green shape, which is labeled “Enzyme.” Above this diagram is the label, “Substrate complex formed.” In b, which is labeled “Induced fit,” two diagrams are shown. The first shows a green wedge-like shape with two small depressions in the upper surface of similar size, but irregular shape. This green shape is labeled “Enzyme.” Just above this shape are two smaller irregular lavender shapes each with a projection from its lower surface. The lavender shape on the left has a curved projection. This projection is shaded orange and has a curved arrow extending from it to the irregular depression just below it in the green shape below. Similarly, the lavender shape on the right has a projection with a pointed tip. This projection is shaded orange and has a curved arrow extending from it to the irregular depression just below it in the green shape below. Two line segments extend from the depressions in the green shape to form an inverted V shape above the depressions. Above this and between the lavender shapes is the label, “Active site changes to fit.” The label, “Substrates” is at the very top of the diagram with line segments extending to the two lavender shapes. To the right of this diagram is a second diagram showing the purple shapes positioned next to each other, fit snugly into the depressions in the green shape, which is labeled “Enzyme.” Above this diagram is the label “Substrate complex formed.” The projections from the lavender shapes match the depression shapes in the green shape, resulting in a proper fit.

discrepancies: Active-site cleft is far too shallow: the source shows two distinct deep pockets (a rounded one and a V-shaped one) that visibly match the substrate pegs, whereas the generated notch is a small shallow zig-zag barely deeper than the outline stroke, so the 'proper shape' fit is not visually convincing.
Enzyme body is wider and flatter than the source's taller, dome/trapezoid silhouette, and the contact patches (pink ellipse, tan triangle) sit on the rim rather than nested inside the pockets.

Left substrate is drawn as a plain rounded rectangle; in the source it is a lollipop-like rounded blob (domed top with a flat inner edge) atop a narrow stem — the squared body changes its recognizable silhouette.

Source shows four side-by-side scenes (free + complex for each model); the generated figure collapses them into one scene driven by a slider/toggle — acceptable, but there is no direct side-by-side comparison of free vs complexed enzyme as the original's composition emphasizes.
Extra annotation not in the source ('active site reshapes' with dashed leader in induced-fit mode) at only 12px, smaller than the rest of the label hierarchy.
evaluation.notes: Recognizable, well-labelled recreation with excellent interactivity (model toggle, binding slider, play animation, ghost outline, 5-step guided demo), but the active-site cleft is far too shallow and the enzyme/substrate silhouettes are squarer and flatter than the source, weakening the visual 'shape complementarity' message.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual structure and interactions are correct; the issues are concrete rendering details (cleft depth, enzyme/substrate silhouettes, contact patch placement, annotation font size) that the generator can fix directly.

attempts.html:
Enzyme–substrate binding

1 / 5 Hover any shape for its name; click for a short explanation.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: The source shows four states side-by-side (unbound + bound complex for each of lock-and-key and induced fit); the default generated view shows only the unbound lock-and-key state, so the side-by-side 'before/after' comparison that is the core of the original composition is only reachable by dragging the slider, never seen simultaneously.

The active-site cleft is noticeably shallower and wider than in the source: in the original the notch is a deep V with a tall thin central spike separating a rounded left pocket and a V-shaped right pocket, whereas the rendered cleft is a shallow dip with barely-visible internal contact patches.
The 'Substrates' leader lines stop short of the substrate bodies (they end in empty space rather than touching each shape, as they do in the source), weakening the annotation link.

Substrate pegs/stems are longer and thinner relative to the substrate bodies than in the source, and the left substrate body lacks the source's tighter rounded-rectangle proportion, making the enzyme look oversized relative to the substrate pair.
Extra annotation not in the source: the dashed 'active site reshapes' callout and 'Show original active-site outline' ghost contour (defensible pedagogically, but additions).
evaluation.notes: Colors, mark types, and labels closely track the source and the interaction set (model toggle, binding slider, play, ghost outline, 5-step demo) is genuinely pedagogical; main weaknesses are a shallower/less articulated active-site cleft and the loss of the source's simultaneous unbound-vs-complex side-by-side composition in the default view.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction set are sound (concept 5, interactivity 5); the remaining issues are concrete execution fixes — deepen/articulate the active-site cleft, extend leader lines to touch substrates, adjust substrate proportions, and default to a side-by-side unbound/bound view.

discrepancies: In the right (complex) scene the substrates sit noticeably higher and larger relative to the enzyme than in the source: their pegs protrude above the rim and the lavender bodies float clear of the olive surface, whereas in the source the two substrate bodies rest directly on the enzyme rim with the pegs fully seated in the notch.

The downward arrows in the left scene are short, free-floating wedges; in the source they are longer arrows that emerge from beside the 'Active site is proper shape' caption and clearly terminate at the two sub-pockets of the cleft, visually tying the caption to the active site.

Enzyme silhouette differs: the source body is a rounded trapezoid with distinct shoulder bumps flanking the cleft and a narrower cleft mouth; the generated body has straighter, near-vertical flanks and a wider, more V-shaped notch with a very tall central spike.

The active-site contact patches are oversized/mis-shaped — the pink patch is a large ellipse sitting high in the cleft rather than the small rounded nub tucked in the left pocket, and the tan triangle is larger than the source's small wedge.

Substrate proportions: the left (boxy) substrate body is drawn much larger than in the source relative to the enzyme, and its peg/tip is longer, making the approaching pair look oversized against the enzyme dome.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-coloured recreation with excellent, conceptually apt interactions (progress slider, play, lock-and-key/induced-fit toggle, ghost outline, 5 narrated steps), weakened mainly by scale issues — oversized substrates/pegs and contact patches and a bound complex that perches above rather than seats into the enzyme rim.
action_items: Scale the substrate bodies and pegs down ~15–20% and lower the bound complex so the lavender bodies rest on the enzyme rim with the coloured tips fully enclosed by the cleft, matching the source's seated complex.
Shrink the pink ellipse and tan wedge contact patches and tuck them into the two sub-pockets of the cleft (source shows small nubs flush with the pocket floors, not a large ellipse near the rim).
Lengthen the two docking arrows and start them just below the 'Active site is proper shape' caption so they clearly point into each sub-pocket, as in the source.
Reshape the enzyme outline toward the source's rounded trapezoid with shoulder bumps flanking a narrower cleft, and reduce the height of the central spike between the two pockets.
